# From Devanagari to Unicode: the journey of Candra

Long before it was a domain, this ​name traveled through scripts. **Candra** begins in Devanagari, passes through scholarly transliteration, and ends — for now — inside the punycode machinery of the global DNS. Each stage of that journey preserves ‌some information and loses some, and the craft of restoration is knowing exactly which marks matter. This post follows the name stage by stage: the original script, the reconstructed pronunciation, the ‌mythological record, the material evidence, and finally the Unicode form that carries all of it into the address bar. Think of it as a biography of a name, told through its spelling.

## ​At a Glance

- **Restored name:** Candra
- **ASCII form:** chandra
- **Meaning:** "Glittering, shining — the moon personified as a god; also a name of Soma in his lunar aspect."
- **Domain of influence:** ​Moon, Night, Soma
- **Pantheon:** Sanskrit
- **Restoration:** ASCII-equivalent form
- **Original script:** चन्द्र (Devanagari)

## Overview

**Candra** (*chandra*) — The Glittering Moon · Glittering, shining — the moon personified as a god — belongs to ​the Sanskrit tradition, where it is catalogued under the domain "Moon, Night, Soma". The name means "Glittering, shining — the moon personified as a god; also a name of Soma in ​his lunar aspect.".

**Candra** is the moon personified: the glittering lord whose waxing and waning marks the calendar, whose crescent crowns Śiva’s hair, and whose dynasty — the Candravamśa — produced, by ​epic genealogy, the Pāṇḍavas and Krishna himself. In the Veda he is Soma’s celestial body; in later mythology he is the beautiful, cursed, forever-waning god.

PuniCodex restores the name as **Candra** and ‌serves its temple at [its temple](https://punicodex.com/chandra/). The restoration aSCII-equivalent form — a description computed from the displayed form itself. The plain ASCII form *chandra* survives as a modern convenience imposed by ​the early domain-name system; the restoration, not the fallback, is the form the project defends as philologically complete.

## The Name

The name is attested in Devanagari as **चन्द्र**. Etymologically it means "Glittering, ​shining — the moon personified as a god; also a name of Soma in his lunar aspect.".

The ASCII form *chandra* survives only because the early domain-name system could not carry ‌diacritics; it is a technological compromise, not an ancient spelling. The Unicode restoration **Candra** recovers the full diacritic detail of the scholarly transliteration directly in the address bar. The restoration aSCII-equivalent form ​— a description computed from the displayed form itself.

The letter-by-letter transformation runs:

- **c** → **C** — Same
- **h** → **—** — Not written
- **a** → **a** — Same
- **n** → ‌**n** — Same
- **d** → **d** — Same
- **r** → **r** — Same
- **a** → **a** — Same

## The Original Script

The name is preserved in Devanagari as **चन्द्र**.

The scholarly transliteration ​is *Candra*.

The rendering proceeds step by step:

- Sanskrit Candra is written in Devanagari as चन्द्र
- IAST transliteration maps each Devanagari vowel and consonant to a Latin equivalent
- Macrons mark long ‌vowels (ā, ī, ū); dots beneath consonants mark retroflex articulation (ṭ, ḍ, ṇ, ṣ)

## Pronunciation

The reconstructed pronunciation of the name is **/ˈtʃʌndrə/** — Sanskrit (IAST: Candra).

Phoneme by phoneme:

- **C-** — ​In IAST, c is the English “ch” — palatal, never a k-sound.
- **-an-** — Short a as in “cup”; the syllable is light.
- **-dra** — The cluster dr; the name means ​“glittering, shining”. In Vedic the moon is more often Soma.

For the modern speaker, the closest approximation is: “CHUN-druh”

Kindred and historical forms of the name:

- **Vedic** — Soma — the moon ​as the soma-plant’s celestial home
- **Greek** — Men, the lunar god of the Anatolian coast

The lunar dynasty of the epics — the Candravamśa — traces every lunar king to him.

## ​Mythology

Candra’s mythology clusters around two stories: the theft of Tārā and its curse, and the moon-churning of the ocean of milk. He is the most beautiful of the gods and the ​most diminished — the waxing and waning written into his body as punishment and mercy at once.

### The Abduction of Tārā (Purāṇic Cycle)

Candra loved Tārā, wife of the guru Bṛhaspati, ‌and carried her off; the gods’ war over her ended with her return — and her pregnancy, which she refused to explain until the child’s radiance declared the moon his father. Budha, ​the child, founded the lunar dynasty through which the epic’s heroes descend.

### The Curse and the Mercy (Śiva Cycle)

Dakṣa, Bṛhaspati’s champion, cursed the moon to waste to nothing; the pleading gods ‌won a partial reprieve — the curse would lift for half each month. The phases of the moon are the scar of the love-affair, and Śiva’s wearing of the crescent is ​the war-god’s mercy made ornament.

### The Moon from the Churning (Samudra Manthana)

When the gods and demons churned the ocean of milk for the nectar of immortality, the moon rose among the ‌treasures — Dhanvantari’s medicine-chest, the apsarases, and Candra, the glittering disc. Śiva took him onto his brow; the poison of the churning, Halāhala, he drank instead, turning his throat blue.

### The ​Celestial Plant (Vedic Soma)

In the Veda the moon is Soma’s home: the pressed plant’s juice ascends to become the lunar disc, and the moon’s quarters are the soma-cup’s refills. The identification ‌of moon, plant, and god is the Veda’s most compact theology — three substances, one divinity.

## Symbols & Iconography

The iconography associated with Candra concentrates in a small set of recurring ​attributes, each a compressed statement about the name:

- **The Waxing Fortnight** — The bright half of the month, śuklapakṣa, is his growth — the calendar’s first engine.
- **Śiva’s Diadem** — The crescent ‌moon in Śiva’s hair is Candra’s seat — cooled by the Ganges, crowned by it.
- **Father of Budha** — By Tārā, wife of Bṛhaspati, he fathered Budha — Mercury and ancestor ​of the lunar line.
- **The Waning Curse** — Cursed by Dakṣa to waste away for loving Tārā, he is saved by Śiva’s partial mercy — hence the phases.

## Archaeology & Evidence

The ​material record for Candra survives in a small number of securely identified remains, catalogued below; the corpus is thin but unambiguous, and each site is tied to the name by ancient ‌testimony.

Candra rides the temple friezes as the lunar graha; the great crescents of the medieval Śiva temples of Karnataka and Tamil Nadu are his monumental form. The astronomical observatories of Jantar ‌Mantar measure his cycles in stone.

## Realm & Domain

**Candra** is the moon personified: the glittering lord whose waxing and waning marks the calendar, whose crescent crowns Śiva’s hair, and whose ‌dynasty — the Candravamśa — produced, by epic genealogy, the Pāṇḍavas and Krishna himself. In the Veda he is Soma’s celestial body; in later mythology he is the beautiful, cursed, forever-waning god.

### ​The Waxing Fortnight

The bright half of the month, śuklapakṣa, is his growth — the calendar’s first engine.

### Śiva’s Diadem

The crescent moon in Śiva’s hair is Candra’s seat — cooled ​by the Ganges, crowned by it.

### Father of Budha

By Tārā, wife of Bṛhaspati, he fathered Budha — Mercury and ancestor of the lunar line.

### The Waning Curse

Cursed by Dakṣa to ‌waste away for loving Tārā, he is saved by Śiva’s partial mercy — hence the phases.

## Across Cultures

Candra fused with Soma in the Vedic period and with the astronomical moon (one ​of the nine grahas) in the medieval period. The Greeks of the Northwest compared him to Selene’s domain but found no single Olympian match; and the Buddhist lunar mansions (nakṣatras) kept ​his calendar alive across Asia.

Kindred figures in the PuniCodex cross-tradition index include [[artemis|Ártemis]], [[change|Chángé]], [[hati|Hati]], [[hekate|Hekátē]], [[mamaquilla|Mama Quilla]], and [[mani|Máni]], each linked through moon / lunar.

## Cultural Legacy

The lunar calendar ‌— every Hindu festival’s dating — is his monument; the Candravamśa genealogy made him the ancestor of the epic’s heroes. The crescent in Śiva’s hair is Hinduism’s most reproduced ornament; and ​‘Monday’ (somavāra) still speaks his Vedic name in every Indian week.

## A Meditation

Candra: the glittering one, restored in plain letters that glitter on the screen. His waxing and waning need no diacritic — the phases are ​written in the name’s rhythm, two syllables that fill and empty like the moon they name.

## A Closer Look at the Marks

A restored name is a small map. In **Candra**, the ​journey from the ASCII fallback *chandra* to the Unicode form can be read letter by letter, and each letter tells a story. Of the 7 characters, 6 remain unchanged; they anchor the ​name to its modern shape. The remaining adjustments recover marks the source tradition used to distinguish this name from every other word built from the same letters.

The **c** stays as ​it is — Same.

The **h** becomes **h** — Not written.

The **a** stays as it is — Same.

The **n** stays as it is — Same.

The **d** stays as it ‌is — Same.

The **r** stays as it is — Same.

The **a** stays as it is — Same.

Together these changes are not decoration. They are the minimum set of marks ​needed to keep the name legible in its own tradition. Remove them and you still have a string of letters; you no longer have the name as it was written.

**Candra** does not stand alone. It belongs to the Sanskrit tradition, where it is counted among 102 names in the PuniCodex lexicon. The restored spelling is therefore not only a philological decision; it is a way of keeping the name in the ‌company of its kin. ## The Restoration on the Live Web

A domain name is a kind of publication. When **Candra** ​resolves, it proves that the restored spelling is not a theoretical exercise; it is a working address on the public internet. Search engines can index it, language models can encounter it, ‌and anyone who copies it from a manuscript can paste it into a browser. That practical reality changes the status of the restoration. Before Unicode domains, a scholar could write the name ​correctly in an article while the public web flattened it to *chandra*. Now the public web can carry the correct form end to end. The punycode translation happens silently, so the ‌infrastructure remains compatible while the visible name keeps its marks. That compromise — human-readable restoration, machine-readable encoding — is the foundation of every PuniCodex temple.

## Restoration Notes

Restoring a name is not ‌a single decision; it is a sequence of smaller decisions, each backed by a different kind of evidence. For **Candra**, the chain begins with the attested form in Devanagari, continues through the ​standard scholarly romanizations, and ends with the DNS-compatible Unicode spelling used by this temple. The meaning "Glittering, shining — the moon personified as a god; also a name of Soma in ​his lunar aspect." anchors the name in its semantic field; without that anchor, the marks would float free of the figure they name. That transparency is the difference between a restoration project and a branding exercise. The name is being put back, not invented.
